comparison: Perfect agreement on fog-induced speed overestimation (C4, C37, C38, C100). Both evaluations support this key finding, with OpenEval citing strong statistical evidence and peer reviewers accepting it as an important contribution without challenge.

Disagreement on behavioral driving results (C5, C52, C55, C104, C144). OpenEval finds claims supported by statistical evidence, but peer reviewers raise uncertainty about haptic feedback confounds from steering wheel that could provide speed information independent of visual perception.

Strong agreement on the key mechanistic finding (C6, C33, C58-C60, C96, C98, C99). Both evaluations support that spatial distribution of contrast, not just global level, determines perceived speed. This represents the core experimental control and theoretical contribution.

Disagreement on stimulus validity (C109, C114-C118). OpenEval finds claims about adequate perceptual information supported by validation data, but peer reviewers express uncertainty about ecological validity, noting impoverished detail compared to real driving and inconsistencies in figures.

Agreement on JND findings (C45, C46, C82, C83, C86). Both evaluations support the discrimination sensitivity results showing higher JNDs for uniform reduction and anti-fog conditions, though peer reviewers had general statistical presentation concerns.

Agreement on replication of uniform contrast reduction effects (C3, C40, C95). Both evaluations support this confirmatory finding, with OpenEval noting it validates the experimental approach and peer reviewers implicitly accepting it as part of the overall contribution.

Disagreement on statistical evidence quality (C35, C36, C41-C43, C54, C75, C80). OpenEval finds statistical reporting appropriate with large effect sizes, but peer reviewers criticize presentation clarity, noting missing ANOVA details, unspecified error bars, and unclear analysis structure.

Agreement on anti-fog perceptual effects (C76-C79, C101). Both evaluations support the finding that anti-fog produces opposite perceptual bias compared to fog, confirming the visibility gradient hypothesis without challenge to the core results.

Partial overlap on anti-fog behavioral results (C88, C89). OpenEval supports behavioral validation of perception-behavior link in Experiment 4, while peer reviewers accepted anti-fog findings generally without specific concerns about these behavioral outcomes.

Agreement on speed variability in anti-fog condition (C92). Both evaluations support this finding, with OpenEval noting greater difficulty maintaining consistent speed and peer reviewers not challenging the variability results.

Disagreement on methodological controls (C161, C162). OpenEval finds methodological details appropriate, but peer reviewers raise uncertainty about contrast adaptation effects, sequence effects over trials, and excessive session duration in Experiment 4.

Disagreement on speed control methodology (C152). OpenEval supports the methodological approach, but peer reviewers question whether haptic feedback from steering wheel was adequately controlled, noting different steering effects at different speeds could provide speed cues.

OpenEval supports the perception-behavior correspondence (C103, C106) across all experiments as converging evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed this integrative claim about the systematic relationship between perceptual and behavioral effects.

OpenEval supports the critique of existing models (C137-C139) for failing to explain opposite effects with identical global contrast. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate this theoretical limitation claim.

OpenEval rates as uncertain the ecological frequency hypothesis for JND differences (C47, C84), noting it remains untested. Peer reviewers did not specifically address this speculative mechanistic explanation.
OpenEval supports claims about prior work on visual field occlusion (C64-C67) as providing theoretical foundation. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate these literature citations.

OpenEval supports the characterization of prior literature consensus (C1, C2, C9-C11, C93, C94) while noting the current study challenges it. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate these literature review claims.

OpenEval supports the critical analysis of prior methodology (C12-C14, C19-C22) distinguishing uniform vs. distance-dependent reduction. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate this methodological critique of prior work.

OpenEval supports the theoretical discussion of neurophysiology and Bayesian models (C119-C136), noting both successes and limitations. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate these theoretical framework claims.

OpenEval supports the logical inference about spatial distribution of visibility in fog (C61-C63) based on physical properties. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate this mechanistic reasoning.
